title: Solar Panel Size for 12V Battery Calculator | Wattlyst
meta: What size solar panel charges a 100Ah or 200Ah 12V battery? Includes charge controller type, sun hours and charging losses.
author: ali-ahmad
anchor: panel watts to charge a 12V battery

sections.h2: What size solar panel do I need to charge a 12 V battery?
p: Work out the energy to put back, then divide by what a panel really delivers. A 100 Ah 12 V lead-acid battery used to 50% needs 100 × 12 × 50% watt-hours, plus the charging loss (85% efficiency). Over 5 peak sun hours at a performance ratio of 0.78, that comes to 181 W, so the panel to buy is 200 W.

The calculator rounds up to the next panel size sold. If the rounding gives you a much bigger panel than the minimum, the charge simply finishes sooner: the time to a full charge is shown for the panel you buy, not for the minimum watts.

sections.h2: Solar panel for a 100 Ah battery and a 200 Ah battery
p: For a 100 Ah 12 V lead-acid battery with 5 peak sun hours the minimum is 181 W, so a 200 W panel with a 30 A MPPT controller. For a 200 Ah battery the minimum is 362 W, so a 400 W panel and a 50 A controller.

These sizes refill a battery used to half each day. If you only use a quarter of the battery, lower the depth of discharge in the advanced options and the panel halves; if you want a day's charge back from a deeper discharge, raise it.

sections.h2: Which charge controller for a 12 V battery: MPPT or PWM?
p: The controller current shown is for an MPPT controller: panel watts ÷ battery volts × a 1.25 margin, rounded up to the next size sold, 30 A for the 200 W panel on a 12 V battery. An MPPT controller converts the panel's higher voltage into charging current, so a higher-voltage panel still delivers its full watts.

A PWM controller is cheaper but wastes the difference between the panel voltage and the battery voltage, so it only works well with a panel made for the battery's voltage and delivers noticeably less than the calculator assumes. If you use PWM, buy a bigger panel or expect slower charging. The charge controller calculator covers PWM sizing by panel current.

sections.h2: Solar charging time calculator: how long to charge the battery?
p: With the panel you buy, the battery refills in 4.5 hours of peak sun, which is 0.9 days at 5 peak sun hours a day. Peak sun hours are not daylight hours: a Pakistani summer day has far more daylight than its five to six peak sun hours, because morning and evening sun is weak.

Lead-acid batteries also slow down in the last part of the charge (the absorption stage), so the real time to a truly full battery is longer than this estimate. Treat it as the time to put back the day's energy, not as a stopwatch.

faq.q: What size solar panel do I need for a 100 Ah battery?
faq.a: A 100 Ah 12 V lead-acid battery used to half needs a 200 W panel (181 W minimum) with 5 peak sun hours a day, and refills in about 4.5 hours of peak sun.

faq.q: What size solar panel for a 200 Ah battery?
faq.a: A 200 Ah 12 V lead-acid battery needs a 400 W panel (362 W minimum) and a 50 A MPPT charge controller to put back half its charge in 5 peak sun hours.

faq.q: How many watts does it take to charge a 100 Ah battery?
faq.a: The energy is 100 Ah × 12 V × the share you used; at 50% with charging losses the panel must deliver about 181 W over 5 peak sun hours. Any panel from 200 W up does it; a bigger panel only charges faster, as long as the controller is rated for it.

faq.q: Which charge controller do I need for a 12 V battery?
faq.a: An MPPT controller rated for the panel watts ÷ battery volts with a 1.25 margin: 30 A for a 200 W panel on a 12 V battery. Also check the controller's maximum panel voltage against the panel's open-circuit voltage.

faq.q: How long does a solar panel take to charge a 12 V battery?
faq.a: The 200 W panel refills a 100 Ah battery used to 50% in about 4.5 hours of peak sun, roughly 0.9 sunny days. Cloud, a dirty panel or a PWM controller make it longer, and lead-acid batteries slow down near full.

faq.q: Is the panel size different for a lithium battery?
faq.a: The formula is the same but the numbers differ: lithium charges at about 95% efficiency and is used to about 90%, so a 100 Ah lithium battery used fully each day needs a 330 W panel. Set the depth of discharge and charging efficiency in the advanced options.

faq.q: Can I connect a solar panel straight to a 12 V battery?
faq.a: Not for daily use. Without a charge controller the panel keeps pushing current into a full battery and boils the electrolyte or damages the cells. Even a small panel should go through a controller.

key_facts: A 100 Ah 12 V lead-acid battery used to 50% needs a 200 W solar panel (181 W minimum) to recharge in 5 peak sun hours.
A 200 Ah 12 V battery needs a 400 W panel and a 50 A MPPT controller under the same sun; doubling the Ah doubles the panel watts.
Solar panel watts to charge a battery = Ah × V × depth of discharge ÷ charging efficiency ÷ (peak sun hours × performance ratio); a panel rarely gives its label watts, so the 0.78 ratio matters.
Lead-acid batteries store about 85% of the energy sent in and should be refilled from about 50%; lithium stores about 95% and can be used to 90%, so a 100 Ah lithium battery needs a 330 W panel.
mistakes: Using daylight hours instead of peak sun hours. A twelve-hour day gives only about five to six hours of full-strength sun, so a panel sized on daylight hours is far too small.
Expecting the label watts from the panel. Heat, dust, cable loss and the controller take their share; the calculator keeps only 78% of the rating.
Matching panel watts to battery Ah with no sun or depth figure. A battery used to a quarter and one drained every day need very different panels for the same Ah.
Using a PWM controller with a high-voltage panel. It clips the panel to the battery voltage and loses a large part of the watts; the controller current here is for MPPT.
Skipping the controller altogether. A panel wired straight to a battery overcharges it once it is full and shortens its life.

fields.name: ah
fields.label: Battery capacity
fields.hint: From the battery label, for example 100, 150 or 200 Ah.

fields.name: volts
fields.label: Battery voltage
fields.hint: A single lead-acid battery is 12 V and a lithium (LiFePO4) one 12.8 V; two lead-acid batteries in series make 24 V.

fields.name: psh
fields.label: Peak sun hours a day
fields.hint: Hours of full-strength sun a day. Pakistani cities get about five to six on a clear day; use four for winter or a cloudy place.

fields.name: dod
fields.label: Depth of discharge to refill
fields.hint: How much of the battery is used each day and must be put back. As a decimal; half for lead-acid, most of it for lithium.

fields.name: charge_eff
fields.label: Charging efficiency
fields.hint: Share of the energy sent in that the battery stores. Lead-acid loses more than lithium. As a decimal.

fields.name: pr
fields.label: Performance ratio
fields.hint: Share of the panel's rated watts you really get after heat, dust, wiring and controller losses. As a decimal.

fields.name: margin
fields.label: Charge controller margin
fields.hint: Sizing margin on the controller current. A decimal like one point two five.

Divided by 5 peak sun hours × 0.78 performance ratio = 181 W minimum, rounded up to the panel sizes sold: 200 W in all, as 1 panel(s) (one when a standard size covers it, else several of the largest). That panel power refills the battery in 4.5 hours of peak sun, about 0.9 sunny days. Controller: 200 W ÷ 12 V × 1.25 margin = 20.8 A, so a 30 A MPPT controller.

examples.title: 100 Ah 12 V lead-acid battery
examples.text: 100 Ah × 12 V × 50% ÷ 85% ÷ (5 h × 0.78) = 181 W minimum, so a 200 W panel. It refills the battery in 4.5 h of peak sun with a 30 A MPPT controller.

examples.title: 200 Ah 12 V lead-acid battery
examples.text: Twice the capacity needs twice the watts: 362 W minimum, so a 400 W panel. Full charge in 4.5 h of peak sun; the controller current is 41.7 A, so a 50 A MPPT controller.

examples.title: 150 Ah battery bank at 24 V
examples.text: Two batteries in series double the volts, so the energy to put back doubles: 543 W minimum, a 550 W panel. At 24 V the controller current stays modest, 28.6 A, so a 30 A MPPT controller; full charge in 4.9 h of peak sun.

examples.title: 100 Ah lithium (LiFePO4) battery used to 90%
examples.text: Lithium stores 95% of what goes in but is used much deeper, 90%, so there is more to put back: 311 W minimum, a 330 W panel, with a 40 A MPPT controller. Full charge in 4.7 h of peak sun.

content.answer: A 100 Ah 12 V lead-acid battery needs at least a 181 W solar panel to put back half its charge in 5 peak sun hours, so buy a 200 W panel with a 30 A MPPT charge controller. That panel refills the battery in about 4.5 hours of peak sun. Panel watts = Ah × V × depth of discharge ÷ charging efficiency ÷ (sun hours × performance ratio).

formula.text: W = (Ah × V × DoD ÷ η_chg) ÷ (PSH × PR); t = (Ah × V × DoD ÷ η_chg) ÷ (W_fitted × PR); A = W_fitted ÷ V × m
lines: W = minimum panel watts; W_fitted = the next panel size sold
Ah, V = battery capacity and voltage
DoD = depth of discharge to put back each day
η_chg = charging efficiency of the battery
PSH = peak sun hours a day; PR = performance ratio
t = hours of peak sun to a full charge
A = MPPT controller current; m = margin

content.safety: Fuse the battery and the panel cable, use a charge controller rated for the panel, keep lead-acid batteries ventilated, and have a licensed electrician or certified installer wire any system that feeds house circuits.
